runs.question: What does `display: contents` do in column pages?
runs.answer:
In a columns tree, `display: contents` is what makes the row of columns work without breaking the DOM tree into something else.

Each page keeps its `$pages` region inside its own view — the DOM stays an ordinary nested tree (a page's children are really nested inside it), and the arrangement contract (`.active-page` / `.active-ancestor` visibility rules, `doc/css.md`) is untouched: a column closes because it lost its mark, not because anything physically moved it out of the tree.

Then, per `doc/columns.md` under "The mechanism": `display: contents` is applied on every descendant *page* and every *region* — it deletes those wrapper boxes from layout, so the only flex items the columns row (`.page-columns-row`) actually sees are the column bodies (`.page-column-body`, built by `column()` in `Page.class.js`). So visually you get peers side by side in a flex row; structurally it's still a tree, several levels deep.

This is asked for at render time, not walked over the tree — `column_host()` in `Page.class.js` does `this.chain().find(page => page.columnar)`, so a page that only loads when you navigate to it still becomes a column the moment it renders, because `render()` checks `column_host()` and calls `render_column(host)` instead of the ordinary page shape.

Two watch-outs tied directly to `display: contents`, from the "What has bitten" section of `doc/columns.md`:
- `:has()` doesn't care whether a `display: contents` element is painted — a closed page is still in the DOM (just contents-collapsed), so the selector that collapses ancestors under a `full` column kept matching after navigating away until the mark itself (`.active-page`/`.active-ancestor`/`.default`) was included in the test.
- The three width tokens (`--page-column-flex`, `-min`, `-max`) are custom properties and inherit through `display: contents` elements same as any other — so a nested `.page.columns` row built inside a `full` column used to inherit its ancestor's values instead of its own defaults, until `.page.columns` was made to reset all three to `initial`.
runs.reason: Correct mechanism, plus render-time column_host and two real watch-outs from the doc: :has() still matching closed pages, and width tokens inheriting through contents.

runs.question: What does `display: contents` do in column pages?
runs.answer:
The mechanism is documented in `public/framework/core/Page/doc/columns.md` (the "The mechanism" section, around text offset ~65666 in the loaded module).

Concretely: `display: contents` is applied to every descendant `.page.column` and every `$pages` region in the column subtree. This deletes those elements' own boxes from layout entirely — they stop being flex items — while leaving the DOM tree itself untouched (`doc/columns.md`: "the DOM is an ordinary nested tree ... `display: contents` on every descendant page and every region deletes those boxes from layout, so the only flex items the row ever sees are the column bodies. Peers on screen, a tree in the DOM.").

So the row layout only ever sees the actual column *bodies* as flex children, even though those bodies are arbitrarily nested pages/regions in the real DOM tree — the intervening wrapper boxes (`.page.column`, `$pages` regions) are made to disappear from the box tree without being removed from the document. A column closes because it lost its mark, not because anything was physically moved (same doc, "The mechanism" intro).

This has a direct consequence noted twice (`doc/columns.md` line ~58092 and the code comment at ~121117 in the column-seam source): because `.page.column` is `display: contents`, it cannot host an event — there's no box to attach a listener/pointer-capture to. That's why the drag "seam" for resizing a column is implemented as a sibling of the body (not a child of it): `column_grab()` puts the seam between the body and the child region so the row itself sees and handles it, rather than trying to put it on the `contents`-collapsed wrapper. The seam also measures 0px so the row's pixel arithmetic still only accounts for the visible column bodies.

The "shape" (which pages become columns) is computed at render time by `column_host()` walking `chain()` — `display: contents` is just the CSS mechanism that makes that logical column tree render as a flat row of peers, not a system that itself decides the tree shape.
runs.reason: Correct, and names the seam consequence: sibling of the body, zero outer size.

runs.question: What does `display: contents` do in column pages?
runs.answer:
`display: contents` deletes a box from layout while keeping it in the DOM. Two places apply it, per `doc/columns.md` under "The mechanism":

1. **Every descendant page's own wrapper** — `render_column()` in `Page.class.js` builds `this.view` as `div.c("page").ac(this === host ? "columns" : "column")`. That `.page.column`/`.page.columns` element is what `Page.css`'s arrangement contract stamps `display: contents` onto (the CSS side of the contract described in `doc/css.md`/`doc/columns.md`'s "The mechanism" section) — so the page tree stays a real nested DOM tree (parent `<div class="page column">` containing child `<div class="page column">`...), but none of those wrapper boxes participate in flex layout.

2. **Every region** (`$pages`) — same rule, so the `page-column-pages` container that holds a column's children is also collapsed out of layout.

Because both the page wrapper and its region are `display: contents`, the only boxes the row's flexbox actually sees are the `.page-column-body` elements (built by `column()`, `Page.class.js`) — the sticky-head-plus-content box each page draws for itself. So structurally you get a real ancestor/descendant DOM tree (columns can close because a class is removed, not because anything was physically moved — "a column closes because it lost its mark, not because anything moved it"), but visually/layout-wise you get a flat row of peer column bodies as flex items.

This is also explicitly why `column_host()` uses `chain().find(...)` (shallowest match) rather than `findLast()`: since nested pages are already flattened into one row by `display: contents`, a columns host nested inside another columns host doesn't get its own row — its subtree just joins the outer row as more peers, because there's only one row of actual flex items regardless of DOM nesting depth.

runs.question: What does `display: contents` do in column pages?

runs.question: How does a url nobody declared get resolved (route() and child())?
runs.answer:
`Page.child(name, levels)` in `Page.class.js` is the resolver. It runs a fixed order of steps for a name that isn't already known, and each one only runs when the name wasn't claimed by an earlier step:

1. **Memory** — `this.children.get(name)`. If a page (or a `null` placeholder from a declared-but-unresolved child) is already there, that wins outright and nothing below runs.
2. **`md` and `fs`** — before anything else, `name === "md"` or `name === "fs"` are handled specially: every page gets an `md/` (its markdown files as pages, via `md_folder()`) and an `fs/` (its real directory, via `fs_folder()`), dynamically imported since core doesn't statically import ext.
3. **`route(name)`** — `const claimed = known === undefined && is.fn(this.route) && this.route(name)`. The `known === undefined` guard is the important part: `route()` only ever gets asked about names the page did *not* declare as a child. A declared child (even one still unresolved, `null`) can never be shadowed by a catalogue route. If `route()` returns a truthy page config, it's added and loaded.
4. **The filesystem probe** — `Page.load(this.url + name + "/", 0)`. This is a dynamic `import(url + "page.js")`. `Page.load` distinguishes "the module doesn't exist" (`Page.missing(error)`, matched against fetch/MIME-type error text) from "the module exists but threw" — only the latter logs an error, so a real syntax error in a page you just wrote doesn't look like a silent 404.
5. **The `.md` fallback** — `Page.file(this.md_dir() + name + ".md")`. If a folder has no `page.js` but a sibling `.md` file, that file becomes the page (title from its first `# `, content rendered by `md.file`). This step is last, so a real `page.js` always wins over a same-named `.md`.

If none of the five hit, `child()` returns `null` and the Router's `load_segments()` walk stops, which is what makes the whole navigation fail (handed to the browser as a real 404/miss).

The doc's framing for *why* it's shaped this way (`doc/declaring.md`): discovery used to be "the declaration is the registration — an undeclared name is a loud 404." That's inverted now — a folder nobody declared **still works when routed to**, because there's no way to list a directory statically, so the probe just tries the one name it was asked for. The cost is real but bounded: one failed `import()` per genuine 404, and nothing at all for a url that resolves.
runs.reason: Mostly right, but it claims a null placeholder in memory 'wins outright'; `if (known)` is false for null, so a declared-unresolved name falls through to the probe.

The `known === undefined` guard is the load-bearing part: `route()` only runs for names the parent never declared. That's what stops a catalogue `route()` from ever shadowing a real declared child — declared always wins, sight unseen. If `route()` returns a config object, `this.add(name, claimed)` builds it as a real child and it's loaded to `levels`.

runs.question: How does `swap_link` keep a doc routed?
runs.answer:
`swap_link`, in `Page.class.js`, draws a `.md` doc inside the current page (over what it was showing) but still gives that swap a real url, so it stays routed rather than becoming an invisible in-place trick.

Concretely:

1. It computes `url = this.swap_url(file)` — `<my url>md/<doc>/` when the file is in my own folder, otherwise the file's module `md/` url (`Page.md_url`).
2. It does `history.pushState({}, "", url + link.hash)` when the current location isn't already that url — so the address bar is honest immediately, before anything even finishes loading.
